question: What is the primary purpose of obtaining a baseline vital sign measurement?

options.A: To calculate the correct dosage of routine vitamins
options.B: To determine the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.C: To diagnose specific infectious diseases immediately
options.D: To provide a reference point for comparing future readings

explanation: A baseline gives the midwife a normal starting measurement for that specific patient so that any dangerous changes later on can be spotted quickly. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why should a midwife allow a newly arrived patient to rest briefly before taking vital signs?

options.A: Physical exertion and anxiety can temporarily alter the readings
options.B: Hospital regulations require a mandatory waiting period for records
options.C: It gives the midwife time to prepare the patient file
options.D: Patients cannot speak clearly immediately upon entering the clinic

explanation: Walking to the clinic or feeling nervous can falsely raise heart rate and blood pressure, so a short rest ensures accurate results. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which temperature route is generally considered the safest and most commonly used for routine adult screening?
explanation: The armpit method avoids mucous membranes, making it safe, non-invasive, and very practical for general clinic use. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why should an oral temperature not be measured immediately after a patient drinks a hot cup of tea?

options.A: Hot fluids cause immediate contraction of the salivary glands
options.B: The hot liquid will falsely elevate the thermometer reading
options.C: It will permanently damage the glass bulb of the thermometer
options.D: The patient will be unable to hold the thermometer under the tongue

explanation: Ingesting hot or cold substances alters the local temperature in the oral cavity, leading to inaccurate results. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h2)

question: What does the term 'rhythm' refer to when assessing a patient's pulse?

options.A: The overall strength and volume of the blood flow
options.B: The total number of beats counted in one full minute
options.C: The specific anatomical site where the pulse is felt
options.D: The regularity or spacing between individual beats

explanation: Pulse rhythm describes whether the heart beats in a steady, even pattern or skips beats irregularly. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h3)

question: A midwife feels a weak, barely perceptible pulse on a woman experiencing severe postpartum hemorrhage. How is this pulse quality best described?
explanation: A weak, thin, and difficult-to-feel pulse is classically described as thready, often seen when blood volume is severely reduced. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why do midwives often count respirations while pretending to continue taking the pulse?

options.A: Hospital protocol strictly forbids looking directly at the patient's chest
options.B: Patients tend to consciously alter their breathing if they know it is being watched
options.C: Patients will accidentally hold their breath if spoken to during this time
options.D: It is mathematically required to calculate the respiratory-pulse ratio simultaneously

explanation: People naturally change their breathing speed and depth when they focus on it, so covert observation yields more accurate baseline data. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following describes tachypnea in an adult patient?

options.A: Deep, labored breathing associated with diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: An abnormally rapid breathing rate above 20 breaths per minute
options.C: An abnormally slow breathing rate below 10 breaths per minute
options.D: A complete and sudden cessation of breathing movements

explanation: The prefix tachy- means fast, so tachypnea refers specifically to a respiratory rate higher than the normal adult range. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h4)

question: What happens to a blood pressure reading if the cuff used is much too small for the patient's arm?

options.A: It has no effect on the final measurement
options.B: It makes it impossible to hear any sounds
options.C: It produces a falsely low reading
options.D: It produces a falsely high reading

explanation: A narrow cuff requires extra pressure to compress the large arm tissue, which artificially inflates the blood pressure numbers. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h5)

question: Where should the midwife place the stethoscope bell when auscultating blood pressure on the arm?

options.A: Across the midpoint of the biceps muscle belly
options.B: On the inner wrist over the radial pulse point
options.C: Directly over the bony prominence of the elbow joint
options.D: Over the brachial artery in the antecubital fossa

explanation: The antecubital fossa houses the brachial artery, making it the correct anatomical site for hearing Korotkoff sounds clearly. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h5)

question: When is the best time for a midwife to record measured vital signs in the patient's case notes?

options.A: At the end of the entire shift before going home
options.B: During the next morning handover meeting
options.C: Only when the patient's condition begins to worsen

explanation: Recording values right away prevents memory lapses and ensures other healthcare workers have access to current data. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which combination of vital sign changes is a classic warning sign of developing hemorrhagic shock in a postnatal woman?

options.A: Falling blood pressure and a rising pulse rate
options.B: Falling temperature and an elevated respiratory rate
options.C: Rising blood pressure and a slowing pulse rate
options.D: Normal blood pressure and a normal respiratory rate

explanation: As blood volume drops, the heart beats faster to compensate, while blood pressure eventually drops as shock progresses. [learn more](BMP119_U2_T2#BMP119_U2_T2_h6)
